newsitem.title: USA: Eastern U.S. senators propose new highway bill.
newsitem.headline: Eastern U.S. senators propose new highway bill.

text.p: A bipartisan group of mostly eastern and northeastern senators on Tuesday introduced a bill to renew highway spending for six years with two key differences from a pending administration transportation bill.
One difference is that the bill allocates highway funds to states more on a need basis that on the administration's basis pegged to the fuel taxes collected in each state.
The other is the amount of money to be spent on roads.

The administration bill introduced last month, a renewal of the Intermodel Surface Transportation Efficiency Act, calls for spending $132 billion as part of its overall $174 billion price tag that also covers mass transit spending.
Road spending in the new bill, introduced by Senate Daniel Patrick Moynihan, a New York Democrat, is set $156 billion.
Aides said both bills allow states to divert highway funds to mass transit in areas hit by traffic congestion and air pollution.

The aides said the Moynihan highway bill, with more than 30 co-sponsors, would be followed by mass transit and Amtrak legislation, and would likely be used as "concept" ideas to be worked into the Clinton bill.
Meanwhile, Congresswoman Susan Molinari, a New York Republican, announced details of a similar House bill, and said she was working for wide backing for the measure.

Some of the supporters of the Moynihan measure told a news conference that the bill was likely to meet strong opposition from senators from the south and west -- areas more dependent on cars -- over the allocation fuel tax money.

Senator Alfonse D'Amato, Republican of New York, a co-sponsor of the measure that reflects the eastern and northeastern need for mass transit spending, predicted that "This will bring out the mother of all battles."

Senator Frank Lautenberg, a New Jersey Democrat, told a news conference that the southern and western states pressing for 95 percernt return for their transportation dollar were guilty of "highway robbery."
He said the bill provides older states with needed funds to costly efforts to preserve existing tranportation systems as well as to fund mass transit and Amtrak to relieve highway congestion.
Another co-sponsor, Senator Joseph Biden, a Delaware Democrat, told the highway lobby, which regularly supports road building, to "lay off, lay off."
He said that if more lanes were added to the already busy Interstate 95 which bisects his small state, the road would take up most of Delaware.

Senator William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said when the finance committee takes up the new transportation bill the measure he would include a proposal to dedicate one-half cent of the federal motor fuel tax to funding for cash-strapped Amtrak.
Among the senators from other regions backing the bill were Carol Moseley-Braun, of Illinois, and Barbara Boxer, of California, both Democrats.
